title: The Late Aftermath
premise: Lena Okafor, a literary translator in her thirties, has spent twelve years in London letting her mother's language — a small Nigerian tongue called Ọ̀ṣun-Ilé — erode word by word, the same language she refused to speak to her dying mother. When a radio broadcast plays a lullaby that was never recorded, sung only once in their kitchen, Lena traces it to a man named Tunde Adewale: her mother's first love, the stranger in the old photographs, and the song's composer. Traveling to Lagos, Lena discovers that her mother's marriage, her own name, and her silence were all shaped by one night of choosing duty over love — and that Tunde is now losing his memory faster than she is losing her words. As she translates his fading songs before they vanish, Lena must finally forgive both strangers in the photographs — him, and the woman her mother became — and choose which inheritance of language and love she will carry home.
about_author: Odile Ishikawa is a former interpreter who grew up between three languages and two continents, and whose essays on translation have appeared in several literary quarterlies. The Late Aftermath is her second novel, written over four years in Lagos, London, and a rented room above a record shop in Ibadan.

chapters.title: Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. In her London flat, Lena finishes translating a novel while realizing she can no longer recall the Ọ̀ṣun-Ilé word for 'threshold.' A phone call from her aunt in Nigeria goes half-understood. The beat is quiet grief disguised as professional competence — a woman fluent in everything except what made her.

chapters.title: The Song That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Driving at night, a radio program on endangered songs plays a lullaby Lena knows was never recorded — composed in her mother's kitchen, sung once. She pulls over, shaking. The emotional beat is vertigo: proof that something private survived outside her memory, that her past exists without her permission.

chapters.title: Inventory of Silence
chapters.summary: Lena's POV, with flashbacks. Lena unpacks her late mother's shipping trunk: photographs of a young man named Tunde, letters in Ọ̀ṣun-Ilé she can only partly read, and a cassette labeled in her mother's hand: DO NOT PLAY. The beat is dread mixed with longing as she decides, against the label, to go to Lagos.

chapters.title: Arrivals
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Lagos overwhelms her — the language everywhere, alive, indifferent to her loss. Her aunt Ngozi receives her coolly, warning that some questions are debts better left unpaid. The beat is displacement: home that refuses to recognize her as its daughter.

chapters.title: The Stranger in the Photograph
chapters.summary: Tunde's POV, introduced for the first time. In a cluttered music shop in Yaba, an aging Tunde tunes a guitar he sometimes forgets he owns, troubled by a melody that returns nightly. His granddaughter notices him writing the same lyric twice. The beat is tender foreboding — we meet the man Lena is hunting before either knows they're looking.

chapters.title: What the Cassette Said
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. At a friend's studio, Lena finally plays the cassette: her mother's voice, young, singing Tunde's lullaby, then speaking — a confession cut off mid-sentence when the tape ends. The beat is devastation; the missing half of the recording becomes the book's engine.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Almost
chapters.summary: Lena's POV, extended flashback. The chapter reconstructs the night Lena refused to speak Ọ̀ṣun-Ilé at her mother's hospital bed, choosing English out of anger. The beat is self-indictment — we see exactly how her silence was built, word by deliberate word.

chapters.title: Finding Tunde
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Following the radio producer's lead, Lena reaches the music shop and stands before Tunde without announcing herself, listening to him play her mother's lullaby wrong — one phrase altered. The beat is suspended recognition; she leaves without speaking, unable yet to claim him or her grief.

chapters.title: The Wrong Note
chapters.summary: Tunde's POV. Tunde senses the woman in the shop knew the song's true form. He asks his granddaughter to find her, fighting the fog that takes names from him daily. The beat is urgency — his memory is a closing door, and he knows it.

chapters.title: Ngozi's Debt
chapters.summary: Aunt Ngozi's POV. Ngozi reveals part of the family secret: Tunde was disowned for loving a woman promised elsewhere, and Lena's mother chose duty — a marriage arranged to protect her family — the very night the lullaby was written. The beat is reluctant witness; Ngozi's coldness reframes as protection.

chapters.title: Translation Session
chapters.summary: Lena and Tunde's alternating POV. They meet formally: she offers to transcribe his songs before they're lost; he agrees, testing her with phrases in Ọ̀ṣun-Ilé she struggles to answer. The beat is wary courtship of trust — two people circling the same wound from opposite sides.

chapters.title: The Lullaby's Second Verse
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Working through Tunde's notebooks, Lena finds a second verse written after her birth — addressed to a child he never met. She realizes he knows who she is and has said nothing. The beat is betrayal folding into tenderness: his silence mirrors hers.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Shop
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Lena demands the truth; Tunde confesses he learned of her years ago and chose not to intrude, believing her mother wanted the past buried. Their argument erupts in the language Lena barely holds. The beat is rupture — the fight itself becomes her largest vocabulary test, and she fails parts of it publicly.

chapters.title: The Night of Choosing
chapters.summary: Tunde's POV, full flashback. The complete story of the night before Lena's mother's wedding: the song, the plea, the refusal — not heartless but terrified, dutiful, loving in the way sacrifice is loving. The beat is tragic comprehension; Lena's mother becomes human rather than villain.

chapters.title: Words Failing
chapters.summary: Tunde's POV. Tunde's memory deteriorates sharply; he forgets the confrontation, then Lena's name, then mistakes her for her mother. Lena, present, answers as her mother would have. The beat is heartbreaking role-reversal — she gets, too late, the conversation she denied her mother.

chapters.title: The Missing Half
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Hunting the rest of the cassette, Lena learns Ngozi kept it hidden for decades because it contains the mother's final message: forgiveness asked for, not given, and a request that Lena be told the truth 'when she can hear it.' The beat is revelation — the silence was inherited, not chosen alone.

chapters.title: Rising Tide
chapters.summary: Lena and Tunde's alternating POV. Racing the fog, they record all of Tunde's songs together; during one session he briefly returns fully to himself and tells Lena he is proud of her — mistaking her still, or perhaps not. The beat is grace under erosion, the book's emotional summit approaching.

chapters.title: Forgiving the Stranger
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. At her mother's grave, Lena speaks in Ọ̀ṣun-Ilé — fluently, fully, for the first time in twelve years — reading aloud the translated lullaby and the finished confession. The beat is catharsis: forgiveness delivered to three people at once, including herself.

chapters.title: The Last Recording
chapters.summary: Tunde's POV. Tunde wakes clear-eyed on a rare good morning and records a spoken letter for Lena, knowing it may be his last lucid hour — telling her the thing he never told her mother: that survival was also a kind of love. The beat is quiet triumph against time.

chapters.title: Threshold
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Tunde dies peacefully weeks later; at the funeral, Lena sings the lullaby correctly, restored note and verse, and the community joins in. The beat is mourning braided with continuity — the song passes through her into living mouths.

chapters.title: The Translator's Choice
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Back in London, Lena declines a prestigious translation contract and instead begins translating Ọ̀ṣun-Ilé songs into English — a project no one commissioned, publishing under her mother's name alongside her own. The beat is resolve: identity rebuilt as a bridge rather than a wall.

chapters.title: The Late Aftermath
chapters.summary: Lena's POV, coda. Years later, Lena teaches her young niece the lullaby, and when the girl asks what the words mean, Lena answers in both languages without hesitation. On the radio, faintly, the recorded songs play. The beat is peace earned, not given — the aftermath, finally, no longer late.
